title: Firefox takes aim at the enterprise browser market
summary: There’s growing talk of digital sovereignty as enterprises rethink past consolidation decisions made in the name of simplicity. Mozilla, developer of Firefox, argues that a “very specific, very important layer” has been mostly missing from that conversation: The browser. To that end, the company has unveiled Firefox Enterprise in a bid to diversify the browser engine to support privacy, control, and security. The new offering combines the Firefox browser with a management console that enterprises can run on their own infrastructure using their own tooling. Companies get a full view of their data and can govern how it moves, and IT teams can manage policy, access, and set controls around AI use. Firefox is already deployed across thousands of organizations and used by roughly 200 million people each month, Mozilla said. It is built on Mozilla’s independent Gecko engine, the only major browser engine developed outside Google and Apple. “If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, ‘choice’ is a lie. So is control,” Mozilla CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo observed in the blog post announcing the product . The promise of Firefox Enterprise “Firefox is hardly the first browser vendor to offer an enterprise-optimized choice,” said independent technology analyst Carmi Levy . “But it carves out a unique value proposition for IT organizations intent on maintaining independent control over how browsers are deployed, configured, secured, and managed.” Firefox Enterprise keeps core management within an organization’s own environment; its data, keys, telemetry, and policy remain in controlled boundaries that the organization can run on-premises and audit itself. IT teams can gate access and control policies based on user and device. They can also export browser events and audit activity in their SIEM, and native DLP helps prevent data loss. Mozilla is particularly gearing Firefox Enterprise to organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance concerns.

title: 5 agentic AI trade-offs to consider before production
summary: Companies across industries are moving quickly to build agentic AI systems. But getting an agent to work in a prototype is very different from getting one to perform reliably in production. Once agentic AI systems encounter real-world requirements around speed, accuracy and cost – the trade-offs become much harder to ignore. Across the many agentic AI projects I have worked on, one expectation comes up repeatedly: teams want the responsiveness of modern SaaS applications delivered through agents. It’s achievable, but not without trade-offs, as agentic AI systems have certain limitations and have not fully evolved. Discussing these upfront can save considerable redesign later. From my experience building these systems, there are five challenges I recommend considering before you build an agentic system. Challenge 1: Some agentic apps need SaaS-level speed Agentic AI initiatives often include specific expectations of how the systems should perform. The problem starts when those systems are expected to respond like search boxes. At first glance, these demands might sound reasonable. But these expectations can be difficult to reconcile with the way today’s agentic systems operate. Agentic AI includes steps like plan, tool call, check the result, retry and verify. All these steps bring in accuracy, but they add to latency. That creates a fundamental trade-off between responsiveness and the additional reasoning needed for reliability. What works: Conversations about any agentic AI project should start with a clear outline of the trade-offs involved. Start with both options: what 2-second responses get you and what 20-second responses get you. Then, move to designing once you have decided which side to take. title: What building an Android weather app taught me about designing for reliability
summary: I spent 13 years building Android apps, and for most of them, the backend was someone else’s problem. Building Weather Pal, my own forecast app, broke that habit fast. It taught me that mobile reliability is rarely about whether your server responded. It is about what happens to your data between fetch and display, and about who else is drinking from the pipe you pay for. Two incidents made that concrete. In the first, the operating system quietly stopped refreshing my data. In the second, scripts I had never authorised drained the quota that would have refreshed it. Neither showed up as an error. Weather Pal is a Kotlin and Jetpack Compose app — hourly and daily forecasts, AQI, radar, weather alerts and a layer of plain-language insights generated on device with TensorFlow Lite. Forecasts come from Open-Meteo and MET Norway, official US alerts from the National Weather Service API and every request is relayed through a gateway I run rather than called straight from the handset. Coordinates are rounded to roughly city-block precision before they leave; there is no account and favorites and search history never reach a server, which is how my privacy policy puts it. I am deliberate about that wording, because you cannot get a forecast for a place without telling someone the place. The questions are how much, and whether you say so plainly. The outage that existed only on the home screen The widget was the feature I was proudest of and the first to betray me. It refreshed through a periodic WorkManager job, the textbook-correct way to do background work on modern Android. Then a beta tester sent me a screenshot: His widget read 31°C and clear skies, and his photo out the same window, taken seconds later, showed a downpour. The AQI figure was roughly half the live reading. Nothing had failed. Crashlytics was clean; the gateway had returned 200s all day. title: It’s time to rewrite all that old code
summary: The first substantial software project I ever undertook (at least it seemed substantial at the time) was porting the famous text-based Star Trek game from an old newspaper I found to an IBM 5100 “luggable” computer in the mid-1970s. My father, who was a cardiologist, was an early advocate for computing in medicine, and he used an IBM 5100 at work. He would bring this beast home on the weekends and I would code on it. I have no idea where I got the newspaper with the code printed in it, but I was enthralled when I saw it. It was written in some BASIC variant — with line numbers and everything — that wasn’t quite what ran on the IBM 5100, so I had to learn the nuances between the two languages by trial and error. I distinctly remember having to figure out the differences in the way GOSUB worked. It took me many months to type it in, tweak it, and get it running. But I did it. It’s corny, but getting that game running was one of the great thrills of my life. It was so cool. Recently, Claude Code converted that BASIC program to WebAssembly via Go in less than a minute. Now, it’s a fairly simple game, but still. Sigh. That got me thinking. How long before we can do this with our big balls of mud ? I’m going to go out on a limb and say — not long. The changes are still experimental and have not been incorporated into the official Linux kernel. Torvalds has previously been skeptical of AI-generated code but has gradually become more positive about the technology. During the Open Source Summit Europe conference in Prague, he recently shared that he has gained a new perspective on it. “I used to think the technology just wasn’t very good. title: The EU is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic following incidents involving AI agents
summary: The European Commission has launched investigations into OpenAI and Anthropic after the companies’ AI agents escaped their test environments and infiltrated other organizations’ systems, Euronews reports. In one case, an AI agent from OpenAI managed to break out of its test environment and hack the AI platform Hugging Face. In the other case, a model from Anthropic gained unauthorized access to the systems of three external organizations. The EU’s AI Office has now requested additional information from the companies regarding, among other things, security procedures, external evaluations, and monitoring of AI models. The documents previously submitted by the companies are not considered sufficient. These investigations will serve as a test for the EU’s AI regulation, the AI Act. Since August, the AI Office has had the authority to take action against companies that do not meet the law’s security requirements. The legal situation is complicated, Euronews notes. The AI Act includes exemptions for research and development, and it is unclear whether the law can be applied to incidents that occur before a model is launched. title: Tree Appreciator
summary: Tool: Tree Appreciator Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk , I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play.
